accent-auto-004.explanation: "e" has an acute accent, "a" has a grave accent.

referenceTranslations: Good evening, how are you doing?
lt-a1m1-001.explanation: "Bonsoir" is the evening greeting; "ça va ?" is the informal question "how are you?".

lt-a1m1-002.explanation: "S'il vous plaît" is the polite "please"; "un café" asks for the item without a verb.

lt-a1m1-003.explanation: In French you say "comment tu t'appelles" (literally "how do you call yourself"); in English the natural way is "what's your name?".

lt-a1m1-005.explanation: To give your age, French uses "avoir" (to have), not "être" (to be) as English does.

lt-a1m1-006.explanation: In the inversion "as-tu", the verb comes before the subject: "quel âge as-tu ?" = "how old are you?" (literally "what age have you?").

lt-a1m1-007.explanation: "Mon" is the masculine possessive ("my"); "s'appelle" means "is called" (a reflexive verb, literally "calls himself").

referenceTranslations: I have a brother and a sister.
I've got a brother and a sister.
lt-a1m1-008.explanation: "Un" is masculine (frère) and "une" is feminine (sœur): the article agrees with the gender of the noun.

accent-a1m1-001.explanation: The "i" in "plaît" has a circumflex accent.

accent-a1m1-004.explanation: The first "e" has a circumflex accent.

referenceTranslations: I would like some cheese, please.
lt-a1m2-001.explanation: "Je voudrais" ("I would like") is the polite way to ask for something; "du" (de + le) means an amount of cheese, "some cheese".

referenceTranslations: Do you drink milk in the morning?
Do you have milk in the morning?
Do you drink milk every morning?

referenceTranslations: I get up at six o'clock.
I wake up at six o'clock.
lt-a1m2-003.explanation: Reflexive verb: "je me lève" is literally "I get myself up"; the time comes with "à ... heures".

referenceTranslations: It's seven o'clock in the evening.
It is seven in the evening.
lt-a1m2-004.explanation: To tell the time, French says "il est sept heures" (literally "it is seven hours"); "du soir" means "in the evening".

lt-a1m2-005.explanation: For the day of the week, French says "nous sommes mardi" (literally "we are Tuesday"); in English you say "today is Tuesday".

lt-a1m2-006.explanation: "Demain matin" means "tomorrow morning"; the present tense "je travaille" can also talk about the near future, like "I'm working tomorrow" in English.

referenceTranslations: I like to listen to music.
lt-a1m6-005.explanation: "Aimer" + infinitive says what you like doing; "de la musique" is the partitive (music in general).

referenceTranslations: Last night I ate an apple.
Last night, I ate an apple.
Yesterday evening I ate an apple.
lt-a1m6-006.explanation: "Hier soir" ("last night") calls for the passé composé: "j'ai mangé" (avoir + the past participle of "manger").

accent-a1m6-007.explanation: The last two "e"s have an acute accent.

cloze-a1m6-001.translation: Yesterday, we ate at the restaurant.
cloze-a1m6-001.explanation: "Manger" forms the passé composé with avoir: nous avons mangé. Most verbs use avoir.

cloze-a1m6-002.translation: Yesterday, she went to the movies.
cloze-a1m6-002.explanation: "Aller" is a verb of movement and uses être: elle est allée. With être, the past participle agrees with the subject (allée, feminine).

cloze-a1m6-003.explanation: The past participle of "faire" is irregular: fait. With avoir, it doesn't agree with the subject, so no -e.

cloze-a1m6-004.translation: This morning, Sophie went to the market.
cloze-a1m6-004.explanation: With être, the past participle agrees with the subject: Sophie is feminine, so allée (with -e). "Aller" is the infinitive, not the past participle.

cloze-a1m6-005.translation: He took the train the day before yesterday.
cloze-a1m6-005.explanation: "Prendre" uses avoir (il a pris), even though it's about traveling: only a small group of movement verbs, like aller, use être. The past participle is irregular: pris.

cloze-a1m6-006.translation: Last weekend, we went to the movies.
cloze-a1m6-006.explanation: "Aller" uses être (nous sommes), and the past participle agrees with the plural subject: allés (with -s).
